\begin{definition}[Bloch--Kato component-assembly map]
\label{def:apparatus:bk-component-map}
For $M_E=h^1(E)(1)$, let
\[
  C_{\mathrm{BSD}}(E)
  =
  \bigl(C_{\mathrm{ht}}(E),C_{\mathrm{an}}(E),C_{\mathrm{fin}}(E),
  \{C_p(E)\}_p,C_{\det}(E)\bigr)
\]
be the integrated BSD carrier, with height/regulator, analytic/period,
finite-source, local $p$-adic and determinant-assembly slots.  The
source-side slot $C_{\det}(E)$ holds an orientation datum and is distinct
from the Bloch--Kato target
\[
  C_{\mathrm{BK}}(E)
  =
  \bigl(M_E,\Delta_f(M_E),z_{\mathrm{BK}}(M_E),\tau_{\mathrm{BK}}(M_E)\bigr).
\]
Suppose given column maps $\rho_{\mathrm{ht}}$, $\rho_{\mathrm{an}}$,
$\rho_{\mathrm{fin}}$, $\rho_p$ and $\rho_{\det}$ into the target, and an
assembly operation that combines one value from each column.  The
component-assembly map
\[
  \rho_{\mathrm{BK}}
  =
  \operatorname{assemble}\Bigl(
  \rho_{\mathrm{ht}},\rho_{\mathrm{an}},\rho_{\mathrm{fin}},
  (\rho_p)_p,\rho_{\det}\Bigr)
  :
  C_{\mathrm{BSD}}(E)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm{BK}}(E)
\]
applies each column map to its own slot and then assembles the results.
Informally, $\rho_{\mathrm{ht}}$ sends height and regulator data to the
global cohomological side; $\rho_{\mathrm{an}}$ sends the leading term and
period to the analytic (zeta-element) side; $\rho_{\mathrm{fin}}$ sends
Tamagawa, torsion, $\Sha[p^\infty]$ and Cassels--Tate data to the finite
determinant side; $\rho_p$ sends local $p$-adic data to the $p$-primary
side; and $\rho_{\det}$ supplies the orientation in the common line.
\end{definition}

normalized_statement: \begin{definition}[Bridge-defect equation] Choose a trivialization of the determinant-line target in which the component comparisons take values in a common additive group, and write $\Delta_{\mathrm{BSD}}^{\mathrm{BK}}$ for the total defect of the BSD comparison. The bridge-defect equation is the decomposition \[ \Delta_{\mathrm{BSD}}^{\mathrm{BK}} = E_{\mathrm{ht/reg}} +E_{\mathrm{an/period}} +E_{\mathrm{finite}} +\sum_p E_p +E_{\det} \] into the height/regulator, analytic/period, finite-source, local and determinant-assembly defects. The local sum is required to be finite: only finitely many $E_p$ are nonzero, and the sum of the local defects is zero when every $E_p$ is zero. Passing between this additive form and the multiplicative form (a total ratio equal to the product of five component ratios) requires a logarithm or trivialization convention that also accounts for signs and units; we do not fix one here. \end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Component-killing] Assume the bridge-defect equation holds in the chosen trivialization. If \[ E_{\mathrm{ht/reg}}=0,\qquad E_{\mathrm{an/period}}=0,\qquad E_{\mathrm{finite}}=0,\qquad E_p=0\ \text{for every }p,\qquad E_{\det}=0, \] then $\Delta_{\mathrm{BSD}}^{\mathrm{BK}}=0$. Equivalently, if $\Delta_{\mathrm{BSD}}^{\mathrm{BK}}\neq 0$, then either some component defect is nonzero or the componentwise comparison (the bridge-defect equation together with its finiteness condition) is not available. \footnote{Lean proves the integer-valued implication, with a supplied value for the local sum and the explicit hypothesis that this value is zero when every $E_p$ is zero; finiteness of the support is one way to guarantee that hypothesis. Declaration names for all formal statements are collected in \Cref{app:formalization}.} \end{theorem}

display_title: The finite scalar factor forgets where a valuation sits
normalized_statement: \begin{theorem}[The finite scalar factor forgets where a valuation sits] Fix a prime $p$. A \emph{finite-source record} at $p$ is a triple of integers $(s,t,u)$, standing for $\bigl(v_p(\#\Sha),\,v_p(\prod_\ell c_\ell),\,v_p(\#E(\Q)_{\tors})\bigr)$, with $s$ even, together with a Cassels--Tate datum $\theta$ from some set with at least two elements. The valuation of the scalar finite factor \[ \phi_{\mathrm{fin}} = \frac{\#\Sha(E/\Q)\prod_\ell c_\ell}{\#E(\Q)_{\tors}^{\,2}} \] defines the readout $q_p(s,t,u,\theta)=s+t-2u$ on records. This readout is not injective: distinct records with different nonzero blocks have the same value, and $q_p$ does not depend on $\theta$ at all. \footnote{Lean proves the statement for this model of the tower, with a two-valued Cassels--Tate tag. Whether the two records below are realized by elliptic curves is not addressed; \Cref{sec:finite-source} gives an arithmetic example for a different readout.} \end{theorem}

normalized_statement: \begin{definition}[Real height-regulator map] Let \[ \Lambda_E=E(\Q)/E(\Q)_{\tors}, \qquad V_E=\Lambda_E\otimes_{\Z}\R, \] and let $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{NT}}$ be the N\'eron--Tate pairing on $V_E$, with associated map \[ h_{\mathrm{NT}}:V_E\longrightarrow V_E^*, \qquad P\longmapsto \langle P,\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{NT}}. \] The real height-regulator map sends the triple $(V_E,\Lambda_E,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{NT}})$ to \[ \rho_{\mathrm{ht/reg}}^{\R} =\det(h_{\mathrm{NT}})\in\det(V_E^*)\otimes\det(V_E)^*. \] If $(P_1,\ldots,P_r)$ is a $\Z$-basis of $\Lambda_E$ and $H_E=\bigl(\langle P_i,P_j\rangle_{\mathrm{NT}}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le r}$ is the Gram matrix, the coefficient of this element in the induced basis is $\det H_E=\Reg(E/\Q)$, with the empty determinant equal to $1$ when $r=0$. The coefficient does not depend on the basis: a change of basis by $A\in\mathrm{GL}_r(\Z)$ replaces $H_E$ by $A^{\mathsf T}H_EA$, and $\det(A^{\mathsf T}H_EA)=\det(A)^2\det H_E=\det H_E$ because $\det A=\pm1$. (A change of basis of finite index $m>1$ multiplies the coefficient by $m^2$, so integrality of the basis matters.) \end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Real height-regulator map]\label{def:apparatus:height-regulator-map}
Let
\[
  \Lambda_E=E(\Q)/E(\Q)_{\tors},
  \qquad
  V_E=\Lambda_E\otimes_{\Z}\R,
\]
and let $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{NT}}$ be the N\'eron--Tate
pairing on $V_E$, with associated map
\[
  h_{\mathrm{NT}}:V_E\longrightarrow V_E^*,
  \qquad
  P\longmapsto \langle P,\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{NT}}.
\]
The real height-regulator map sends the triple
$(V_E,\Lambda_E,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{NT}})$ to
\[
  \rho_{\mathrm{ht/reg}}^{\R}
  =\det(h_{\mathrm{NT}})\in\det(V_E^*)\otimes\det(V_E)^*.
\]
If $(P_1,\ldots,P_r)$ is a $\Z$-basis of $\Lambda_E$ and
$H_E=\bigl(\langle P_i,P_j\rangle_{\mathrm{NT}}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le r}$ is
the Gram matrix, the coefficient of this element in the induced basis is
$\det H_E=\Reg(E/\Q)$, with the empty determinant equal to $1$ when $r=0$.
The coefficient does not depend on the basis: a change of basis by
$A\in\mathrm{GL}_r(\Z)$ replaces $H_E$ by $A^{\mathsf T}H_EA$, and
$\det(A^{\mathsf T}H_EA)=\det(A)^2\det H_E=\det H_E$ because
$\det A=\pm1$.  (A change of basis of finite index $m>1$ multiplies the
coefficient by $m^2$, so integrality of the basis matters.)
\end{definition}

normalized_statement: \begin{theorem}[Height tangent Schur collapse] Let $r\ge1$ and let $H$ be a positive definite real symmetric $r\times r$ matrix. Identify a symmetric variation $\delta H$ with its coordinate vector $x=\operatorname{vech}(\delta H)\in\R^n$, $n=r(r+1)/2$, listing the entries $\delta h_{ij}$ with $i\le j$. Then \[ D_H(\delta H) = d(\log\det)_H(\delta H) = \tr(H^{-1}\delta H) = d_Hx, \] where the row $d_H$ has entry $(H^{-1})_{ii}$ at each diagonal coordinate and $2(H^{-1})_{ij}$ at each off-diagonal coordinate $i<j$. Take the audit energy $C=I_n$ on these coordinates and the full source $L_{\mathrm{full}}(x)=x$. Then \[ \KDD=\|d_H\|^2, \qquad \XiC=d_Hd_H^{\mathsf T}-d_H\,I_n\,d_H^{\mathsf T}=0 . \] For $r=0$ the tangent space is zero, $n=0$, and $\KDD=0$: the rank-zero row is vacuous. \footnote{Lean proves the algebraic core: for every row $d$ of every length over any commutative ring, the identity source gives Schur residual zero, and the identity matrix is the unique matrix satisfying the four Penrose equations at the identity. For $r=2$ it also proves that the displayed row computes $\tr(H^{-1}\delta H)$ when $\det H\neq0$. The calculus step identifying the row with the derivative of $\log\det$, and the general-rank row, are proved here on paper.} \end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Height tangent Schur collapse]\label{thm:apparatus:height-schur-collapse}
Let $r\ge1$ and let $H$ be a positive definite real symmetric $r\times r$
matrix.  Identify a symmetric variation $\delta H$ with its coordinate
vector $x=\operatorname{vech}(\delta H)\in\R^n$, $n=r(r+1)/2$, listing the
entries $\delta h_{ij}$ with $i\le j$.  Then
\[
  D_H(\delta H)
  =
  d(\log\det)_H(\delta H)
  =
  \tr(H^{-1}\delta H)
  =
  d_Hx,
\]
where the row $d_H$ has entry $(H^{-1})_{ii}$ at each diagonal
coordinate and $2(H^{-1})_{ij}$ at each off-diagonal coordinate $i<j$.
Take the audit energy $C=I_n$ on these coordinates and the full source
$L_{\mathrm{full}}(x)=x$.  Then
\[
  \KDD=\|d_H\|^2,
  \qquad
  \XiC=d_Hd_H^{\mathsf T}-d_H\,I_n\,d_H^{\mathsf T}=0 .
\]
For $r=0$ the tangent space is zero, $n=0$, and $\KDD=0$: the rank-zero
row is vacuous.%
\footnote{Lean proves the algebraic core: for every row $d$ of every
length over any commutative ring, the identity source gives Schur
residual zero, and the identity matrix is the unique matrix satisfying
the four Penrose equations at the identity.  For $r=2$ it also proves
that the displayed row computes $\tr(H^{-1}\delta H)$ when
$\det H\neq0$.  The calculus step identifying the row with the derivative
of $\log\det$, and the general-rank row, are proved here on paper.}
\end{theorem}

Let $r_{\mathrm{an}}=\operatorname{ord}_{s=1}L(E,s)$ and \[ A_E=\frac{L^{(r_{\mathrm{an}})}(E,1)}{r_{\mathrm{an}}!}\neq0 \] be the analytic leading coefficient, that is, the leading Taylor coefficient of $L(E,s)$ at $s=1$. Let $\Omega_E^+>0$ be the real period in the BSD normalization: the integral of $|\omega_E|$ over $E(\R)$ for a N\'eron differential $\omega_E$. The native analytic/period family is the pair \[ L_{\mathrm{an/per}}(E)=(A_E,\Omega_E^+), \] and the real analytic/period map is \[ \rho_{\mathrm{an/period}}^{\R}:(A_E,\Omega_E^+)\longmapsto (A_E/\Omega_E^+)\,e_{\mathrm{an/per}}, \] where $e_{\mathrm{an/per}}$ is a basis vector of a real line. \begin{definition}[Real analytic/period map]\label{def:apparatus:analytic-period-map}
By modularity~\citep{Wiles1995,BreuilConradDiamondTaylor2001},
$L(E,s)=L(f_E,s)$ extends to an entire function.  Let
$r_{\mathrm{an}}=\operatorname{ord}_{s=1}L(E,s)$ and
\[
  A_E=\frac{L^{(r_{\mathrm{an}})}(E,1)}{r_{\mathrm{an}}!}\neq0
\]
be the analytic leading coefficient, that is, the leading Taylor
coefficient of $L(E,s)$ at $s=1$.  Let $\Omega_E^+>0$ be the real period
in the BSD normalization: the integral of $|\omega_E|$ over $E(\R)$ for a
N\'eron differential $\omega_E$.  The native analytic/period family is the
pair
\[
  L_{\mathrm{an/per}}(E)=(A_E,\Omega_E^+),
\]
and the real analytic/period map is
\[
  \rho_{\mathrm{an/period}}^{\R}:(A_E,\Omega_E^+)\longmapsto
  (A_E/\Omega_E^+)\,e_{\mathrm{an/per}},
\]
where $e_{\mathrm{an/per}}$ is a basis vector of a real line.  The column
contains no height, torsion, Tamagawa or $\Sha$ data.
\end{definition}

normalized_statement: \begin{definition}[Real finite-source map] The finite-source tower is $C_{\mathrm{fin}}(E)=C_{\mathrm{Tam}}\oplus C_{\tors}\oplus C_{\Sha[p^\infty]}\oplus C_{\mathrm{CT}}$, with native family \[ L_{\mathrm{finite}}(E) = \Bigl((c_v(E))_{v\mid N},\ E(\Q)_{\tors},\ \bigl(S_p,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{CT},p}\bigr)_p\Bigr), \qquad S_p=\Sha(E/\Q)[p^\infty]/\Sha(E/\Q)[p^\infty]_{\mathrm{div}}, \] where $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{CT},p}:S_p\times S_p\to\Q/\Z$ is the perfect alternating Cassels--Tate pairing. Throughout this section we assume that $\Sha(E/\Q)$ is finite. Then each divisible part is zero, $S_p=\Sha(E/\Q)[p^\infty]$, only finitely many $S_p$ are nontrivial, and $\prod_p\#S_p=\#\Sha(E/\Q)$. The real finite-source map is the product of three factors: \[ \rho_{\mathrm{finite}}^{\R} = \rho_{\mathrm{Tam}}^{\R} \otimes \rho_{\tors}^{\R} \otimes \bigotimes_p \rho_{\Sha\text{-}\mathrm{CT},p}^{\R}, \] with $\rho_{\mathrm{Tam}}^{\R}=\prod_{v\mid N}c_v$, where $c_v=\#E(\Q_v)/E^0(\Q_v)$; $\rho_{\tors}^{\R}=\#E(\Q)_{\tors}^{-2}$; and \[ \rho_{\Sha\text{-}\mathrm{CT},p}^{\R}\bigl(S_p,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{CT},p}\bigr)=\#S_p . \] The last factor has an integral description. If an alternating integer matrix $A$ presents $S_p$ (that is, $S_p\cong\operatorname{coker}A$) with linking form $(x,y)\mapsto -x^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}y \bmod \Z$ equal to the pairing, then $\#S_p=|\det A|=\Pf(A)^2$. For example, the hyperbolic plane $H_n=(\Z/n\Z)^2$ with $\langle(a,b),(c,d)\rangle=(ad-bc)/n \bmod \Z$ is presented by $A=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&n\\-n&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, with $|\Pf(A)|=n$ and $\#H_n=n^2$. \end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Real finite-source map]\label{def:apparatus:finite-source-map}
The finite-source tower is
$C_{\mathrm{fin}}(E)=C_{\mathrm{Tam}}\oplus C_{\tors}\oplus
C_{\Sha[p^\infty]}\oplus C_{\mathrm{CT}}$, with native family
\[
  L_{\mathrm{finite}}(E)
  =
  \Bigl((c_v(E))_{v\mid N},\ E(\Q)_{\tors},\
  \bigl(S_p,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{CT},p}\bigr)_p\Bigr),
  \qquad
  S_p=\Sha(E/\Q)[p^\infty]/\Sha(E/\Q)[p^\infty]_{\mathrm{div}},
\]
where $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{CT},p}:S_p\times S_p\to\Q/\Z$ is the
perfect alternating Cassels--Tate pairing.  Throughout this section we
assume that $\Sha(E/\Q)$ is finite.  Then each divisible part is zero,
$S_p=\Sha(E/\Q)[p^\infty]$, only finitely many $S_p$ are nontrivial, and
$\prod_p\#S_p=\#\Sha(E/\Q)$.  The real finite-source map is the product
of three factors:
\[
  \rho_{\mathrm{finite}}^{\R}
  =
  \rho_{\mathrm{Tam}}^{\R}
  \otimes
  \rho_{\tors}^{\R}
  \otimes
  \bigotimes_p \rho_{\Sha\text{-}\mathrm{CT},p}^{\R},
\]

\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Real $p$-adic map]\label{def:apparatus:p-adic-map}
Let $T=T_pE$ and $V=V_pE=T\otimes\Qp$, as representations of $G_{\Qp}$,
and suppose $E$ has good reduction at $p$.  The finite local
condition~\citep{BlochKato1990,Fontaine1994} is
\[
  \Hf(\Qp,V)
  =
  \ker\bigl(H^1(\Qp,V)\to H^1(\Qp,V\otimes B_{\mathrm{cris}})\bigr).
\]
Since $1$ is not an eigenvalue of Frobenius on $D_{\mathrm{cris}}(V)$, the
Bloch--Kato exponential
$\exp_V:D_{\mathrm{dR}}(V)/\operatorname{Fil}^0D_{\mathrm{dR}}(V)\to\Hf(\Qp,V)$
is an isomorphism of one-dimensional $\Qp$-vector spaces; its inverse is
the logarithm
\[
  \log_V:\Hf(\Qp,V)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
  D_{\mathrm{dR}}(V)/\operatorname{Fil}^0D_{\mathrm{dR}}(V).
\]
If $E$ has good ordinary reduction~\citep{Mazur1972}, with ordinary
filtration $0\to T^+\to T\to T^-\to0$, the native ordinary family is
\[
  L_p^{\mathrm{ord}}(E)=\bigl(T^+,\ \Hf(\Qp,V),\ \log_V\bigr).
\]
If $p$ is odd and $E$ has good supersingular reduction with $a_p=0$, the
native signed family~\citep{Kobayashi2003,Pollack2003} is
\[
  L_p^{\pm}(E)=\bigl(H^1_+,\ H^1_-,\ \kappa_\pm\bigr),
\]
where $H^1_\pm$ are Kobayashi's plus and minus local conditions (at a
specified level of the cyclotomic tower, with specified coefficients) and
$\kappa_\pm$ are the corresponding plus and minus Coleman maps.  Other
supersingular cases, including $p=2$, are outside this definition.

These native families consist of $p$-adic objects.  A real local map
\[
  \rho_{p,\mathrm{ord}}^{\R}:L_p^{\mathrm{ord}}(E)\longrightarrow
  \Delta_f(V,T)_{p,\R}^{\mathrm{ord}},
  \qquad
  \rho_{p,\pm}^{\R}:L_p^{\pm}(E)\longrightarrow
  \Delta_f(V,T)_{p,\R}^{\pm},
\]
reading them in a real line, is \emph{not} constructed here.  It requires
a rational structure on the relevant $p$-adic determinant lines (for
example on the line of $\log_V$), and in the signed case a choice of
specialization or localization of the Iwasawa-theoretic Coleman maps
together with a normalization.  We treat these real readouts as supplied
data, part of the local transport of \Cref{obl:apparatus:rho-p-transport}.
The calculations below only concern which native coordinates such a
readout is allowed to see.
\end{definition}

normalized_statement: \begin{theorem}[Five-column to Bloch--Kato scalar contraction] In the coordinates $x=(x_{\mathrm{ht}},x_{\mathrm{an}},x_{\mathrm{fin}},x_p,x_{\det})\in\R^5$, the orientation-normalized scalar readout of \Cref{def:apparatus:five-column-tensor} is $\Phi_{\mathrm{5col}\to\mathrm{BK}}(x)=d\cdot x$ with $d=(1,1,1,1,0)$. \begin{theorem}[Five-column to Bloch--Kato scalar contraction]\label{thm:apparatus:five-col-bk-comparison}
In the coordinates
$x=(x_{\mathrm{ht}},x_{\mathrm{an}},x_{\mathrm{fin}},x_p,x_{\det})\in\R^5$,
the orientation-normalized scalar readout of
\Cref{def:apparatus:five-column-tensor} is
$\Phi_{\mathrm{5col}\to\mathrm{BK}}(x)=d\cdot x$ with $d=(1,1,1,1,0)$.
With the full typed source $L(x)=x$ and $C=I_5$,
\[
  \Xi_{\mathrm{5col}\to\mathrm{BK}}
  =
  \|d\|^2-d\,I_5\,d^{\mathsf T}
  =
  4-4=0,
\]

direction $e_{\det}=(0,0,0,0,1)$ lies in the kernel of

\end{theorem}

display_title: The Gram matrix forgets provenance data
normalized_statement: \begin{theorem}[The Gram matrix forgets provenance data] Fix $E/\Q$ of Mordell--Weil rank $r\ge2$ and a set $\mathcal P$ of provenance data with at least two elements (for example, records of which cycle construction is claimed to produce each basis class). Define a \emph{cycle-source record} to be a Mordell--Weil basis $(P_1,\ldots,P_r)$ of $\Lambda_E$ together with an element of $\mathcal P$. The map sending a record to its Gram matrix $\bigl(\langle P_i,P_j\rangle_{\mathrm{NT}}\bigr)_{i,j}$ is not injective. In particular, the Gram matrix, which determines $\Reg(E/\Q)=\det(\langle P_i,P_j\rangle_{\mathrm{NT}})$, does not determine the provenance data. \footnote{Lean proves a narrower record-model statement: the projection from records consisting of an integer Gram identifier and three Boolean metadata fields to the identifier is not injective. It constructs no Mordell--Weil bases, height matrices or cycle classes.} \end{theorem}

display_title: A finite window does not decide a universal statement
normalized_statement: \begin{theorem}[A finite window does not decide a universal statement] Let $\mathcal C$ be the set of isomorphism classes of elliptic curves over $\Q$, and consider assignments $\tau:\mathcal C\to\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$, thought of as truth values of some property of curves. Let $U(\tau)$ be the statement ``$\tau(E)=\mathrm{true}$ for every $E$''. \begin{enumerate} \item No function of the restriction $\tau|_W$ computes $U(\tau)$ for all assignments $\tau$: the assignment $\tau_1\equiv\mathrm{true}$ and the assignment $\tau_2$ that agrees with $\tau_1$ except at one curve $E_*\notin W$, where it is false, have the same restriction to $W$, but $U(\tau_1)$ is true and $U(\tau_2)$ is false. \item In Schur form, let $\mathcal C(B)$ be the finite set of curves of conductor at most $B\ge960$, with $M(B)=\#\mathcal C(B)$ coordinates. The window source is the coordinate projection onto the five coordinates in $W$, and the residual against the identity readout on $\mathcal C(B)$ has trace $M(B)-5$, which tends to infinity with $B$.\footnote{Lean proves both parts for a model in which curves are indexed by natural numbers and the window is the first five indices: the two completions agree on the window, differ outside it, are separated by the universal target, and are identified by every function of the window; and the residual trace $M-5$ takes every natural-number value. The model says nothing about which truth assignments arise from actual properties of curves.} \end{enumerate} \end{theorem}

\mathrm{false}\}$, thought of as truth values of some property of curves.

\item No function of the restriction $\tau|_W$ computes $U(\tau)$ for all
  assignments $\tau$: the assignment $\tau_1\equiv\mathrm{true}$ and the
  assignment $\tau_2$ that agrees with $\tau_1$ except at one curve

  $U(\tau_1)$ is true and $U(\tau_2)$ is false.
\item In Schur form, let $\mathcal C(B)$ be the finite set of curves of

display_title: A finite set of primes does not decide all-prime coverage
normalized_statement: \begin{theorem}[A finite set of primes does not decide all-prime coverage] Let a \emph{coverage record} assign to each prime $p$ a status, covered or uncovered, and let the all-prime target be the statement that every prime is covered. For every finite set $P_0$ of primes there is a prime $q\notin P_0$, and there are two coverage records that agree at every prime of $P_0$, such that the first covers every prime and the second leaves $q$ uncovered. Consequently no function of the restriction of a record to $P_0$ decides the all-prime target. \footnote{Lean proves the statement for coverage records indexed by natural numbers, with an explicit prime $q$ dividing $1+\prod_{p\in P_0}p$, and with primality decided by a finite divisor check. These are formal records; no claim is made that they arise from elliptic curves.} \end{theorem}

quantities above (for curves, $\R$).  Assume $C\neq0$ and $d\neq0$.

  \longrightarrow

\]

\begin{enumerate}

\item A set $k$ of scalars with an element $0$ and operations $-$,

    \qquad
    (a/d)\cdot b=(a\cdot b)/d ,

  $L^*=L^{(r)}(E,1)/r!$, the order $\#\Sha(E/\Q)$, the regulator
  $\Reg_{\mathrm{NT}}(E)$, the period $\Omega_E$, the Tamagawa product
  $\Tam(E)$ and the squared torsion order $d=\#E(\Q)_{\tors}^{\,2}$.

  \[
    R_E=\frac{\#\Sha(E/\Q)\,\Reg_{\mathrm{NT}}(E)\,\Omega_E\,\Tam(E)}{d},

display_title: Sensitivity does not make a hypothesis necessary
normalized_statement: \begin{remark}[Sensitivity does not make a hypothesis necessary] One might hope to argue from \Cref{thm:closure:composite-signature} that each recognition hypothesis is needed, since each ``governs'' a factor. The argument fails. In rank at least $2$, the hypothesis $\GammaGZ$ with its normalization already implies $L^*=R_E$ (\Cref{sec:recognition-sources}), so deleting $\GammaPD$ and $\GammaSP$ does not affect the scalar conclusion. Sensitivity of the product to its factors says nothing about which hypotheses are needed to prove an identity between the product and another number. A genuine independence statement needs an interface in which the factors are introduced before they are normalized. Suppose native factors $a$ and $b$ satisfy \[ N:\ L^*=a\,\Reg\,\Omega\,b,\qquad C_b:\ b=\Tam(E),\qquad C_a:\ a=\#\Sha(E/\Q)/d . \] Then $N$, $C_a$ and $C_b$ together imply $L^*=R_E$, and none of the three can be dropped: with $\Reg=\Omega=\#\Sha=d=\Tam=1$, the triples $(L^*,a,b)=(2,1,2)$, $(2,2,1)$ and $(2,1,1)$ satisfy exactly two of the three premises and violate the identity, since $R_E=1\neq2=L^*$. But this independence is a property of the premises, not of the identity: when $\Reg\,\Omega\neq0$ and $N$ holds, $L^*=R_E$ is equivalent to the single equation $ab=(\#\Sha/d)\Tam(E)$, which can hold while both $C_a$ and $C_b$ fail (take $a=2$, $b=1/2$ and all other values $1$). With all values positive, the solutions are exactly $a=u\,\#\Sha/d$, $b=\Tam(E)/u$ for $u>0$. Lean checks these countermodels and the classification over $\Q$. None of these rational models is an elliptic curve, and we draw no arithmetic conclusion from them. \end{remark}

\begin{enumerate}

normalized_statement: \begin{theorem}[The constructed and imported entries] In the register of the shell, the construction of the shell and the normalization of $\kapr$ have status by construction, and the three comparison inputs have status approved external input. Moreover, if the quantities are integers or lie in a field (with the shell's multiplication being the field multiplication) and $C=\Omega_E\Reg\,\Tam(E)\neq0$, then one has $\kapr C=sC$ if and only if $\kapr=s$, for every $s$ (for $s=\#\Sha/\#E(\Q)_{\tors}^{\,2}$ this is the normalization of $\kapr$); and the asserted components of the three inputs hold. \footnote{Lean proves the status assignments and the cancellation, the latter for integer-valued quantities; the components of the inputs are returned from the input records. Lean does not show that the inputs are approved in any sense beyond this label.} \end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The constructed and imported entries]\label{thm:closure:aor-mechanical-records}
In the register of the shell, the construction of the shell and the
normalization of $\kapr$ have status by construction, and the three
comparison inputs have status approved external input.  Moreover, if the
quantities are integers or lie in a field (with the shell's multiplication
being the field multiplication) and $C=\Omega_E\Reg\,\Tam(E)\neq0$, then
one has $\kapr C=sC$ if and only if
$\kapr=s$, for every $s$ (for $s=\#\Sha/\#E(\Q)_{\tors}^{\,2}$ this is
the normalization of $\kapr$); and the asserted components of the three
inputs hold.%
\footnote{Lean proves the status assignments and the cancellation, the
latter for integer-valued quantities; the components of the inputs are
returned from the input records.  Lean does not show that the inputs are
approved in any sense beyond this label.}
\end{theorem}

normalized_statement: \begin{theorem}[The recognition entries] In the register of the shell, each of the three recognition hypotheses is an atom of residual type \emph{source}, with secondary types role, target, transport and limit, and with status bridged; none has status zero. The asserted content of the three recognition records holds. \footnote{The formalization records this as a conditional schema: the statuses are read off the register, and the asserted content is returned from the records.} \end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Refinement-stable closure of the register] The register of the shell is closed, and every refinement of it is closed. The recognition entries satisfy \Cref{thm:closure:aor-recognition-discharge}, and, when $\Omega_E\Reg\,\Tam(E)\neq0$ in the setting of \Cref{thm:closure:aor-mechanical-records}, so do the constructed and imported entries. \footnote{Lean proves this for the refinement relation just described, which it shows to be reflexive and transitive and to preserve statuses. It does not formalize the general refinement relation of the AOR framework.} \end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Refinement-stable closure of the register]\label{thm:closure:aor-instance}
The register of the shell is closed, and every refinement of it is
closed.  The recognition entries satisfy
\Cref{thm:closure:aor-recognition-discharge}, and, when
$\Omega_E\Reg\,\Tam(E)\neq0$ in the setting of
\Cref{thm:closure:aor-mechanical-records}, so do the constructed and
imported entries.%
\footnote{Lean proves this for the refinement relation just described,
which it shows to be reflexive and transitive and to preserve statuses.
It does not formalize the general refinement relation of the AOR
framework.}
\end{theorem}

display_title: What the register does and does not say
normalized_statement: \begin{remark}[What the register does and does not say] Closedness of the register means that every residual difficulty has been given a status other than ``eliminated''. Three of them are bridged: they are carried as recognition hypotheses, which this paper does not prove. The register therefore records an accounting of the conditional theorem, not a proof of Strong BSD. Its stability is proved only for the declared refinement relation, and the label ``approved'' on an input is not a verification of that input. \end{remark}
